summary:
Moon View is an interactive site for exploring the Moon and comparing possible landing locations. It brings lunar terrain, sunlight, Earth and satellite visibility, and slope information together in one place. It is designed to be approachable for everyone: it can support an early, preliminary comparison of sites, while also giving space enthusiasts ways to explore the lunar surface and imagine what astronauts will experience when they will visit those sites.

The site also includes a demo gamification concept: landing-site scores and a leaderboard make it fun to compare locations and observation windows. These features are for exploration and illustration, not validated mission rankings or proof that a location is safe to land on.
details:
What the project does and how it works

Moon View is an interactive website for exploring the Moon and comparing potential landing sites. It displays 3D lunar terrain and estimates when the Sun, Earth, and selected satellites are visible from a location. Users can compare locations over a chosen period, view local horizons, and use the Explore tab for an immersive, first-person-style view from the surface.

The project combines elevation data from the USGS Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) with sky-position data from JPL Horizons. It uses terrain to estimate shadows, visibility, and slope. The landing scores and leaderboard are a demonstration concept—not certified safety ratings—and some example layers are synthetic.

Benefits and intended impact

The site makes lunar terrain and visibility easier for a general audience to explore. It can support preliminary comparison of locations and help users understand how terrain, sunlight, and line of sight may affect a site. Its intended impact is educational and exploratory: making lunar surface conditions more tangible without suggesting that the results replace expert analysis or mission planning.

Tools and development

The project uses Python for data processing and calculations, with Flask serving the website. The interface uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, including Three.js for 3D views and Plotly for interactive visualizations. It relies on public lunar elevation and ephemeris data, and runs in a web browser on a computer with an internet connection. No specialized hardware was developed or required.

What makes it creative and what the team considered

Moon View brings scientific data, interactive 3D exploration, comparative site assessments, and a playful leaderboard together in one experience. The Explore view helps users picture themselves at a lunar location, while the scoring demo gives them an approachable way to compare sites.

Key considerations included making the tool accessible to both enthusiasts and people interested in early site comparisons; accounting for terrain, slope, shadows, time, and visibility; and clearly communicating that some outputs are estimates or demonstrations rather than measured composition data or mission-grade assessments.
